---
title: "Colorado Net Migration by Age"
subtitle: "1990 to 2025"
---

The Census Bureau publishes county population by age, and it publishes total net
migration by county, but not net migration *by age* below the state level. This
site estimates it as a demographic residual: for each cohort, net migration is
whatever is left once observed births and deaths are removed from the population
change.

$$
\text{NM}(c) = \text{Pop}_{\text{end}}(c) - \text{Pop}_{\text{start}}(c) - \text{Births}(c) + \text{Deaths}(c)
$$

Four periods are covered — **1990–2000, 2000–2010, 2010–2020 and 2020–2025** —
for Colorado and each of its 64 counties. Cohorts are keyed by **age at the end
of the period**, so a group labelled 25–29 in 2010–2020 is the people who were
25–29 in 2020 and 15–19 in 2010. Keying on the ending age means every group has
a real age, including the children born along the way.

## The headline

Colorado's net migration has swung widely — about 71,800 a year in the 1990s,
31,900 in the 2000s, 45,000 in the 2010s, and 28,300 since 2020. But the *shape*
of who came has changed far more than the total.

| Age at end of period | 1990–2000 | 2000–2010 | 2010–2020 | 2020–2025 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 5–9 | 18.3 | 4.3 | 8.3 | 4.3 |
| 10–14 | 20.0 | 11.2 | 9.5 | 2.0 |
| 20–24 | 30.4 | 11.2 | 12.9 | 14.8 |
| **25–29** | **38.4** | **19.0** | **26.9** | **36.3** |
| 30–34 | 33.4 | 15.9 | 27.6 | 19.3 |
| 40–44 | 16.4 | 5.5 | 7.9 | 2.2 |
| 50–54 | 11.2 | 2.3 | 1.3 | −4.2 |
| 60–64 | 6.4 | 1.5 | −0.2 | −5.9 |
| 70–74 | 4.2 | 2.0 | −0.5 | −4.7 |

: Annual net migration per 1,000 people {.striped tbl-colwidths="[28,18,18,18,18]"}

In the 1990s Colorado gained people at **every single age**, from infants to the
very old — the weakest group still ran at nearly 4 per 1,000 a year. Nothing
since has looked like that.

Today the peak is almost back to 1990s height: 25–29 runs at 36.3 per 1,000 a
year against 38.4 in the boom. But the base beneath it has fallen away. Every
group from 45–49 upward is now **negative**, and the flow of school-age children
has all but stopped.

So the state is not drawing fewer young adults than it used to. It is drawing
almost exactly as many, and far fewer of everyone else. Where Colorado once
attracted families and retirees alongside its twenty-somethings, it now
attracts the twenty-somethings and loses the rest.

## Caveat

The Census and SDO county age estimates are themselves cohort-component output,
built from these same vital records plus the agencies' own migration signals.
This recovers the net migration by age *implied by* those published estimates. It
is the right number for anyone working from them, but it inherits their
assumptions rather than testing them.
